Su esplendor es la segunda mitad del XIX, con el Canario, la Trini, Baldomero Pacheco y Fosforito el Viejo; también firmaron malagueñas el Mellizo, único gitano creador de una (inspirada en el prefacio de la misa), y Chacón. Diego Clavel recogió treinta y una en los noventa. La rondeña, de principios del XIX y de la tierra del Tobalo, es la pieza con que muchos guitarristas abren sus conciertos; la jabera, ruda y difícil, debe su nombre a una vendedora de habas y está casi perdida; los verdiales, de probable raíz morisca, apenas han cambiado y conservan la panda con violín, panderos, chinchines y cañas para la fiesta de san Juan.

scenes.name: Los tanguillos de Cádiz
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Vinculados al carnaval de Cádiz, son el soporte de chirigotas, coros y murgas; cantados en grupo pierden su naturaleza flamenca, que es individual, aunque como baile la conservan. Hay constancia de los «tangos graciosos» del barrio de La Viña en 1779, en la tonadilla La anónima de Tomás Abril, y el tango americano o de negros terminó de formarlos. Letras jocosas y satíricas: «el chiste ingenuo y feliz enfrente de la tragedia jonda del quejío» (Emilio Jiménez Díaz). Aurelio y Pericón de Cádiz, Manuel Vargas y la Perla los grabaron en la primera mitad del siglo XX, y hasta Mairena dejó dos. Chano Lobato, su mayor cultor, los elevó a cante noble y recrea la venta de los cuadros que popularizó Pericón.

scenes.name: Las tonás: martinetes, carceleras y deblas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Cantes sin acompañamiento, prueba de su antigüedad, en cuartetas octosílabas de intensa carga dramática y origen gitano indiscutible: son crónicas de la miseria, la cárcel y la persecución. Demófilo ya las daba en 1881 por «cantes viejos casi caídos en desuso»; en el siglo XIX hubo entre veintisiete y treinta y cuatro, cada una con el nombre de su creador. La más antigua es la de Tío Luis el de la Juliana, aguador y primer cantaor del que hay noticia (segunda mitad del siglo XVIII), conservada por Antonio Chacón y recreada por Pepe de la Matrona; se le atribuye también la toná de los pajaritos, que recuerda la tonada sefardí de los bilbilicos. Los martinetes toman el nombre del martillo de la fragua, aunque es difícil cantar mientras se forja: Tío Juane de Jerez montaba una fragua en escena en los setenta y ochenta, y Antonio el Bailarín creó su baile con martillo y yunque; la familia fragüera más antigua es la de los Cantorales de Cádiz, que Silverio visitaba. Las carceleras cantan la prisión y servían para pasar mensajes en romaní desde las rejas. La debla, único palo con nombre romaní («diosa»), es religiosa, casi perdida y muy difícil; llegó a hoy por Tomás Pavón en los cuarenta y la recuperó Antonio Mairena.

scenes.name: Las sevillanas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Nacen de las seguidillas castellanas, que en Sevilla se hicieron más vivas y fáciles de repetir: cuatro coplas para bailar en pareja un galanteo, con temas andaluces, amorosos o rocieros (corraleras, rocieras, bíblicas, de feria, marineras, romeras). Lorca recogió una del siglo XVIII. Su gran auge comercial llegó en los setenta, con millones de discos que daban envidia a los flamencos; las han grabado con jondura Manuel Vallejo, la Niña de los Peines, la Paquera de Jerez, el Turronero, Chiquetete y Camarón.

scenes.name: El fandango
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Muy apreciado por su musicalidad y fácil de interpretar, no es un palo básico pero no es menor: la vieja división entre cantes grandes y chicos está obsoleta, y la jondura la pone el intérprete, no la antigüedad del palo. Canto para bailar de origen muy antiguo e incierto (Corominas lo deriva del portugués fado; hay quien le ve un lejano origen árabe), aparece por escrito en un entremés de 1705 y lo describe el deán Manuel Martí en 1712; en el siglo XIX fue el cante y baile nacional español, y a finales de siglo se aflamencó en Andalucía y dejó de bailarse. De él salen las granaínas, las malagueñas y los cantes de Levante, y hay fandangos propios en Lucena, Cabra, Puente Genil, Jaén, Granada o Almería. Su apogeo en la ópera flamenca lo desprestigió tanto que a cantaores como Pepe Menese les parece un insulto que se lo pidan; desde los años ochenta se revaloriza.

facts.title: Sexual Identity Declaration (1972)
facts.body: Six months before the release of *The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and The Spiders from Mars*, David Bowie declared himself to be gay. Given that homosexuality had only been decriminalized in England in 1967, this public confession from a major pop star had a huge liberating effect on individuals afraid to reveal their own sexual orientation. "Six months before the album came, a Bowie declared himself to be gay."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: Debut of Ziggy Stardust (July 8, 1972)
facts.body: On July 8, 1972, David Bowie introduced the world to his character Ziggy Stardust at the Royal Festival Hall in London. This marked the genesis of the "world's first synthetic, pre-packaged, ultra-theatrical rock star," lasting 360 days and becoming a highly influential piece of marketing and PR in rock history. "That night, David Bowie stepped on stage at the Royal Festival Hall in London and introduced himself by saying, hi, I'm Ziggy."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: Public Homosexuality Confession (1972)
facts.body: On January 22, 1972, David Bowie made a shocking declaration to a British music tabloid reporter, stating, "I'm gay and I always have been." While such a statement is common today, in 1972, it was highly controversial and made him the first major rock and roll musician to publicly profess his homosexuality.
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: Contractual Dispute with Main Man (1972-1975)
facts.body: David Bowie wanted out of his contract with Tony DeFries' management company, Main Man, by the end of 1974, just two years into their relationship. Despite selling millions of albums, Bowie realized that most of the profits were not reaching him, suspecting that the new contract signed with Main Man at the end of September 1972 was "weird." On January 29, 1975, Bowie informed RCA, his record label, of his intention to split from DeFries, sparking a battle over who owned Bowie's next album.
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Mighty Managers of Rock
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: Peele Session (May 23rd, 1972)
facts.body: David Bowie, accompanied by his band The Spiders from Mars, recorded a session for DJ John Peel on May 23rd, 1972. These "Peele Sessions" were a notable part of BBC programming, allowing artists to record live off the floor to circumvent "Needle Time" restrictions. "Here's something from May 23rd, 1972, when an artist on the asset named David Bowie dropped in for a session with his band, The Spiders from Mars."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: "Coming Out" Statement and LGBTQ+ Impact (1972)
facts.body: In January 1972, Bowie gave a "flippin' quote" to a British music paper, stating he had "always been gay." This statement, unthinkable for a celebrity at the time, given the legal context of homosexuality in Britain (decriminalized in England/Wales only in 1967, still illegal in Scotland/Northern Ireland for years, and military ban), became a bomb. Despite Bowie later recanting claims of being gay or bisexual, this declaration resonated with thousands who were afraid to come out, giving them courage. "This coming out struck a chord with thousands of people who wanted to do the same thing but were too afraid."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Remembering David Bowie: Part 1
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: NME Interview Coming Out (1972)
facts.body: On January 22nd, 1972, Bowie gave an interview to the NME, a major British weekly music tabloid, where he famously stated, "I'm gay and I always have been." While later acknowledged as a publicity stunt, the impact of those seven words was immense and incalculable, giving hope to closeted individuals globally. "I'm gay and I always have been."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Early Days of LGBTQ Rock
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: Melody Maker Interview (January 1972)
facts.body: In early 1972, Bowie gave a front-page interview to British music weekly Melody Maker, titled "Oh, You Pretty Thing." The article described his image as a "swishy queen, a gorgeously effeminate boy," noting his "camp" demeanor while he maintained he was "ungay." This interview showcased his deliberate push for shocking outrage and sexual ambiguity. "He gave an interview to Melody Maker, one of the big British music weeklies. The title of the article was, oh, you pretty thing."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: Ziggy Stardust Debut (February 1972)
facts.body: David Bowie formally debuted the Ziggy Stardust character on February 10, 1972, at the Torquay Jug Pub in London. At the time, he was still a minor pop star, resulting in low attendance, but this performance marked the beginning of Ziggy's ascent. "Then on February 10th, 1972, David Bowie debuted the Ziggy character at the Torey Jug Pub in London."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: Top of the Pops Performance (July 6, 1972)
facts.body: Bowie's seminal performance on Top of the Pops on July 6, 1972, with The Spiders from Mars, was highly influential. Dressed in a quilted jumpsuit, red boxing boots with green laces, and bright red-orange hair, Bowie's anisocoria (permanently dilated pupil from a childhood fight) added to his "otherworldly look." His public display of affection towards guitarist Mick Ronson (draping his arm around his shoulders) was considered "super duper gay" for the era and had a profound impact, leading to the immediate appearance of "Ziggy Clones" and helping young people feel accepted in their sexuality. "One especially interesting performance was on top of the pops on the BBC, July 6th, 1972."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: A Clockwork Orange Soundtrack (1972) as Landmark
facts.body: The soundtrack for Stanley Kubrick's *A Clockwork Orange*, composed by Wendy Carlos (then Walter Carlos) using modular synthesizers, became a landmark in the development of electronic music for the masses. Its completely electronic and unheard sounds inspired rock musicians seeking new and different artistic directions. "It became a landmark in the development of electronic music for the masses."

facts.title: Amazing Grace the Film Technical Glitch (1972)
facts.body: The documentary filmed during the *Amazing Grace* sessions by Sidney Pollock suffered a major technical glitch: the filmed footage and audio were not synced, and no clapperboards were used to fix it in post-production. This led to the film being shelved for over four decades, only seeing release in 2018 after both Pollock and Franklin had passed away, thanks to 21st-century technology resolving the misalignment. "The filmed footage and the audio were not synced up, and Pollock had not used clapperboards to make it fixable in post-production. Amazing Grace the Film would wind up sitting on a shelf for more than four decades, until after both Pollock and Aritha Franklin had died, and 21st century technology made it possible to fix the audio video misalignment."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Say a Little Prayer Edition Part 2
facts.name: Aretha Franklin

facts.title: Pre-Release Presentation to Critics (February 1972)
facts.body: Nearly a year before the official release of *The Dark Side of the Moon*, in February 1972, Pink Floyd held a presentation in London where they showcased a significant portion of the melodies and songs that would form part of the album. This preview was for specialized press and critics, who were reportedly amazed by what they heard, yet had to wait a full year for the album's launch. "casi un año antes, en febrero de 1972 o un año antes de que saliese el álbum, la banda ya había hecho una presentación en Londres en la que había presentado una parte importante de las melodías y de las clasiones que formaban parte del dance, ahí lo hacemos, a toda la brecha especializada e incluso algunos críticos."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan

facts.title: Planned Anti-Nixon Tour (1972)
facts.body: John Lennon planned an ambitious anti-Richard Nixon tour for 1972, intending to follow the President around the country and conclude with a three-day music festival outside the Republican National Convention in Miami. This plan, however, never materialized as Lennon's legal troubles and the attention of the FBI, instigated by Senator Strom Thurmond, led to a deportation attempt. "He thought, you know, maybe I could do a tour. An anti-Richard Nixon tour in 1972 and follow Richard Nixon around the country."

facts.title: Wall of Sound (1972)
facts.body: The Grateful Dead pioneered concert amplification with their "Wall of Sound" setup in 1972, which represented a significant breakthrough in modern concert sound. This system generated at least 26,000 watts, and possibly up to 30,000 watts, marking a massive leap in power and clarity for live music and establishing new standards for large-scale concert sound. "when it comes to modern day concert amplification, it was the grateful dead who really broke through with their wall of sound setup in 1972."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Big Picture Stuff: Part 2
facts.name: The Grateful Dead

facts.title: Early Sound System Inadequacy (1972)
facts.body: In 1972, The Grateful Dead held a meeting in their Novato, California, warehouse practice space to discuss the inadequacy of their concert sound. Their system, designed by Bob Hyal in 1968, utilized Alltec's "Voice of the Theater" series cabinets, radial horns (a novel inclusion at the time), ring tweeters, and a custom crossover, and while "better than most," it was deemed "lacking by 1972" for the band's needs.
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Concert Sound
facts.name: The Grateful Dead

facts.title: Development of the Wall of Sound (1972-1973)
facts.body: Following the realization that their existing system was inadequate, The Grateful Dead's crew embarked on a year-long experimentation with PA gear, led by Owsley "Bear" Stanley. Their efforts culminated in the unveiling of the revolutionary "Wall of Sound" in 1973, a system designed to drastically improve live sound. "Over the next year, their crew experimented with PA gear, led by a former ballet dancer from Kentucky turned LSD drug dealer name Ausley Bear Stanley."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Concert Sound
facts.name: The Grateful Dead

facts.title: Strategic Hiatus (1972-1976)
facts.body: Neil Diamond deliberately stayed off the stage for four years between 1972 and 1976, aiming to learn from the experiences of artists like Elvis Presley and The Beatles. He believed that constant public presence could lead to an artist becoming "public property" and wished to maintain his independence. "He actually said he tried to learn a little something from Elvis and the Beatles. He said, I think if you're out in front of the public too much, if you're too recognized, too well known, you do in a sense become public property. I always wanted to be my own man."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 39 - American Top 40 - Keeping Our Feet on the Ground and Reaching for the Stars (Part 1)
facts.name: Neil Diamond

facts.title: Alien Rock Star Narrative
facts.body: This album, released in 1972, was hugely influential and served as Bowie's commercial breakthrough, appealing to glam kids and future punk rock figures. It tells the story of an alien rock star named Ziggy, a name inspired by Bowie's friend Iggy Pop and Texas proto-psychobilly singer Norman O'Dan (The Legendary Stardust Cowboy). The music was originally intended for a full-on musical, stage show, or BBC TV program. The narrative describes a dying Earth five years in the future, with Ziggy initially ignored, then discovering "the Infinite's" (spacemen) who promise salvation, leading Ziggy to believe he is a prophet. Upon the Infinite's arrival, Ziggy dies on stage after contact due to their antimatter composition, after which the now-visible Infinite's absorb his essence. This album dramatically presented rock and roll theatrically with costumes, concept, and playacting, a style previously unseen. "The album tells the story of an alien rock star named Ziggy."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Rock Opera
facts.body: This rock opera was released in the late spring of 1972 and details the story of Ziggy Stardust, an omnisexual rock star sent to Earth five years before its demise due to resource depletion. Ziggy is a messenger from the Starman, tasked with delivering a message of peace and love, but he is ultimately destroyed after believing too much in his own importance as a prophet. The album was added to the National Registry of the Library of Congress in 2016 for its historical and cultural significance. "Ziggy Stardust is an omnisexual rock star who is sent to Earth five years before it dies due to the people of Earth depleting its natural resources."

facts.title: A Clockwork Orange (1972) Score
facts.body: Wendy Carlos, a classical musician who had been collaborating with Bob Moog on the development and application of his new modular synthesizers, was hired by director Stanley Kubrick to compose the score for his 1971 futuristic dystopian film, *A Clockwork Orange*. The entirely electronic score, released as a soundtrack in 1972 (with Carlos identifying as Walter Carlos at the time), introduced sounds no one had heard before and became a landmark in the widespread development of electronic music, influencing many rock musicians seeking novel sounds. "No one had ever heard such sounds. It was completely electronic."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Rolling Stone Interview and Image Control (1972)
facts.body: In a 1972 interview with Robin Green for *Rolling Stone*, Cassidy was initially hostile, fearing ridicule. He discussed his image and the expectations placed upon him two years into playing Keith Partridge, admitting his resistance to cutting bubblegum records. To challenge his bubblegum image and assert his desire to be a rock star, he posed nude for an Annie Leibovitz photo shoot for the magazine's cover. "He talked about his image and what was expected of him by that time two years into playing Keith Partridge. He told the interviewer Robin Green. When I first got in the studio, I said to the producer West Farrell, I don't want to cut bubble gum records and he said, no man, we're going to cut bubble gum records."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s

facts.title: Original Motion Picture Soundtrack
facts.body: Curtis Mayfield eagerly wrote this soundtrack to comment on life in the ghetto and provide perspective on both drug users and pushers. It sold five million copies and can stand alone from the movie. Music critic Vince Aletti noted that Mayfield moved away from typical soundtrack conventions, with songs commenting on the film's action rather than merely illustrating it, and lyrics not restricted to the title track. The album blends influences from funk, blues, jazz, and rock, reflecting the diverse nature of American cities. "This Mayfield said that he was eager to write for the Superfly soundtrack because he wanted to add to the commentary on life in the ghetto and offer a glimpse of what the victims and the drug pushers both may have felt."

facts.body: This song, released in 1972, became one of pop's most famous and best diss records, rising to number one in January 1973. Carly Simon has maintained mystery about the full identity of the "you" it targets, though she clarified it's not about ex-husband James Taylor or Mick Jagger (who sings backup). She later revealed that the middle verse, describing the vain man taking advantage of a naive singer, is about actor Warren Beatty. The song's genius lies in its meta-diss nature, explicitly stating, "I bet you think this song is about you," and its immense popularity, sending her album "No Secrets" to number one. "But your so vain rose all the way to number one in January 1973."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

facts.body: This song, released in November 1972, became a genuine Top 40 hit and an AM radio success on both sides of the Atlantic, despite its "raunchy references." The lyrics recounted true stories of individuals in Andy Warhol's circle, including Holly Woodlawn (a transsexual from Miami), Candy Darling (another transsexual), and Joe Campbell, referred to as the "Sugar Plum Fairy." The first version of the song was recorded with drumsticks, but it was later re-recorded using brushes to achieve a "smoky, sleazy nightclub feel." The saxophone part at the end was played by Ronnie Ross, who had taught David Bowie saxophone in the 1950s. The iconic sliding bass line was created by session player Herbie Flowers, who layered two bass lines—one from a stand-up double bass and another from a fretless electric. Flowers was reportedly paid $30 for his contribution, and the bass line has since been sampled countless times in hip-hop and dance songs worldwide. "Released in November 1972 and an AM radio hits on both sides of the Atlantic, despite all the raunchy references that's Lou Reed and walk on the wild side."
